rawText: Introduce a caching layer so that high-traffic short-code-to-long-URL lookups are served from cache rather than from the database on every request, reducing database load and improving redirect latency for popular links.
normalizedProblem: Introduce a caching layer so that high-traffic short-code-to-long-URL lookups are served from cache rather than from the database on every request, reducing database load and improving redirect latency for popular links.

acceptanceCriteria.description: A short-code resolution that is served from cache must not perform a database read for that request.
A cache hit must return the same long URL that a direct database lookup would return (i.e., no stale or incorrect redirects).
On a cache miss the system must fall back to the database, return the correct long URL, and populate the cache for subsequent requests.
If a short URL is deleted or its destination is updated, the cache entry must not serve the old mapping beyond the defined TTL or invalidation window.
The p99 redirect latency for a cached short code must be measurably lower than the p99 latency for the equivalent database-only lookup under equivalent load.
Database read throughput (queries per second) for short-code resolution must decrease when popular links are being resolved under load.
A short code that does not exist in the database must not be cached as a valid mapping (negative-result caching policy must be explicitly decided).
Cache failures (e.g., cache node unavailable) must not cause resolution to fail; the system must degrade gracefully to direct database lookups.

ambiguities: The requirement says 'popular links' but never defines what makes a link popular (e.g., a request-rate threshold, a fixed whitelist, most-recently-used eviction, or top-N by hit count). It is unclear whether all links are cached or only a qualifying subset.
'Basically never changes once it exists' implies updates are rare but possible. The acceptable staleness window (if any) after an update or deletion is not stated.
It is not specified whether caching should apply to all redirect types (301 permanent, 302 temporary, etc.) uniformly, or differ by redirect type.

The requirement does not say whether the cache should be in-process (application memory), a shared external cache (e.g., Redis/Memcached), or a CDN edge cache. Each has different consistency and operational implications.
No target latency improvement or cache-hit-rate target is given, making it ambiguous what 'faster' means quantitatively.
assumptions: PROPOSED: All short codes are eligible for caching (not only a predefined 'popular' subset), with eviction governed by a standard policy such as LRU or LFU so that the working set naturally reflects popular links.
PROPOSED: A TTL-based invalidation strategy is used (e.g., cache entries expire after N minutes), with an active cache-invalidation call also issued whenever a link is updated or deleted.
PROPOSED: Cache misses and cache errors are both observable via existing metrics/logging infrastructure so the cache hit rate can be monitored.
PROPOSED: The cache is a shared external store (e.g., Redis) rather than per-instance in-process memory, to ensure consistency across multiple application instances.
outOfScope: Changes to how short codes or long URLs are created, updated, or deleted (beyond any invalidation hooks needed for cache correctness).
Analytics or click-counting changes — only the resolution/redirect path is in scope.
CDN or browser-level caching strategies (unless later confirmed in scope).
Rate limiting or abuse prevention for high-traffic links.
Any UI or API surface changes.
